content: The national vaccination campaign introduced a routine three-dose infant vaccination series and conducted a mass catch-up campaign during 1999–2000, targeting all individuals aged 12 months to 17 years. The serogroup C conjugate meningococcal vaccines used in this campaign were licensed based on safety and immunogenicity data, but without clinical efficacy data. By 2001–2002, vaccine coverage in the United Kingdom was estimated to be 80% among infants, 84% among toddlers, 76% among preschoolers, and 86–87% among school-aged children. The vaccine's effectiveness within the first year of administration ranged from 88% to 98% across different age groups. However, there is insufficient data to differentiate the efficacy of the three meningococcal conjugate vaccines. Since the campaign began only in 1999, long-term data on the duration of protection are not yet available. Among infants who received three doses of the vaccine at 2, 3, and 4 months of age, vaccine efficacy declined to -81% (95% CI = -7,430 to 71) after just one year. Although the number of cases remains low, likely due to vaccine-induced herd immunity, this finding raises concerns about the meningococcal vaccine schedule and the potential need for a booster dose. During 1999–2000, carriage rates of group C meningococci in the United Kingdom declined by 66%. Additionally, the incidence of meningococcal serogroup C disease decreased by 67% among unvaccinated individuals aged 1–17 years and by 35% among unvaccinated individuals over 25 years of age, indicating the additional benefit of herd immunity. The quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4), licensed for use in the United States in January 2005, contains 4 µg of capsular polysaccharide from serogroups A, C, Y, and W-135 conjugated to 48 µg of diphtheria toxoid in a 0.5-mL single dose. MCV4 is available only in single-dose vials. Studies conducted among U.S. military recruits in the 1960s demonstrated that the absence of naturally acquired bactericidal antibodies, as measured by a serum bactericidal antibody assay (SBA) using intrinsic human complement, was associated with susceptibility to meningococcal group C disease. SBA titers greater than 4, measured using human serum as an exogenous complement source (hSBA), are considered the standard correlate of clinical protection against serogroup C meningococcal disease. Serogroup C conjugate meningococcal vaccines were licensed in the United Kingdom based on safety and immunogenicity data, without clinical efficacy data. The immunologic data supporting the use of these vaccines were generated using a serum bactericidal assay with baby rabbit complement (rSBA). Threshold values were validated by comparing rSBA titers with those obtained using hSBA. For licensure in the United Kingdom, rSBA titers greater than 128 were considered predictive of protection. However, only 60% of rSBA titers in the range of 8–64 corresponded to hSBA titers greater than 4.
